newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia hopes for peaceful election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia hopes for peaceful election campaign.

text.p: Indonesian leaders called on Friday for a peaceful general election campaign as concern over possible violence before the May 29 national and local polls continued to hit the nation's currency.

Official reassurances came at an early morning pre-campaign ceremony involving officials and leaders of the three sanctioned parties as the rupiah slid further against the dollar before stabilising in late morning trade.

"We hope the election campaign will go smoothly," said Interior Minister Yogie Memet, speaking as head of the General Election Institute (LPU), which oversees the campaign opening on Sunday and the polls.

After weeks of violence between rival political factions in populous Central Java province, money market dealers said the foreign exchange markets remained nervous and operators continued to go long on dollars as uncertainty prevailed.
Spot rupiah fell to a low of 2,440 rupiah against the dollar on Friday morning after an opening of 2,432.50, but later stablised at 2,438.
"People keep buying the dollar as they try to factor in possible riots or unrest during the campaign," one local bank dealer said.
Armed forces commander General Feisal Tanjung said authorities had anticipated any problems.

"We are ready. There will be no riots. All is safe," Tanjung told reporters after the LPU ceremony, which included the Javanese traditional cutting of a large cone of cooked rice to bring good fortune for the election.
All wings of the military and police have conducted high-profile training exercises to prepare for any contingency, including riots, hostage-taking and bomb threats.
Further exercises were planned in the capital on Friday.

Despite the recent clashes between supporters of Golkar and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) in Central Java, Tanjung said there were no sensitive provinces where trouble was expected.
The political temperature increased in Central Java early this year after its governor ordered public buildings and objects to be painted yellow, the colour of Golkar.
The move led to retaliation by supporters of the PPP and Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), which repainted public objects white or red and white.
Clashes in various towns have escalated in recent weeks as each attack sparks retaliation from the other side.
Golkar's general chairman, Information Minister Harmoko, said the ruling party was expecting an orderly 27-day official campaign.
Golkar is seeking just over 70 percent of the vote from the 124.7-million-strong electorate after receiving 68 percent in the 1992 elections. The PPP got 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent in 1992.
